nodes.name: Self-consistent formulation of quantum mechanics in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space
nodes.statement: Hence, a self-consistent formulation of quantum mechanics in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space is an ongoing problem \cite{Weyl1950, Schwinger1960, Schwinger2003, Pearle1973, Santhanam1976, Jagannathan1981, Gudder1981, Jagannathan1982, Jagannathan1983, Gudder1985, Gudder1986, Busch1993, Galetti1999, Hakioglu2000, DelaTorre2003a, DelaTorre2003b, Vourdas2004, Gazeau2006, Revzen2008, Bang2009, Sasaki2011}, especially considering quantum information science, quantum optics, and physics of the Planck length, where finite-dimensionality finds new horizons.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: A self-consistent finite-dimensional formulation of quantum mechanics is an ongoing open problem.

nodes.name: Weyl's characterization of the canonical commutation relation
nodes.statement: \left| \langle x \ket{p} \right|^2 = \mbox{const} \Longleftrightarrow \commut{ \hat{x}, \hat{p} } = i \hbar,
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
nodes.statement_short: Constant $|\langle x|p\rangle|^2$ is equivalent to the canonical commutation relation $[\hat{x},\hat{p}]=i\hbar$.
nodes.label: PhysOrigin_CCR

nodes.name: No bounded operators obey the canonical commutation relation
nodes.statement: The left-hand side of Eq. (\ref{PhysOrigin_CCR}) is well defined in a finite-dimensional space, whereas the right-hand side of Eq. (\ref{PhysOrigin_CCR}) is not because no bounded operators obey the canonical commutation relation \cite{Weyl1950, Reed1980}.
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
nodes.statement_short: The commutator side of Weyl's relation is undefined in finite dimensions since no bounded operators satisfy $[\hat x,\hat p]=i\hbar$.
conclusions: no bounded operators obey the canonical commutation relation

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional coordinate and momentum operators (mutually unbiased bases)
nodes.statement: Thus, in the literature on finite-dimensional quantum mechanics, the coordinate and momentum operators are usually defined as those whose eigenvectors obey \begin{align} \langle x_n \ket{p_k} = \exp(i2\pi n k /N) / \sqrt{N}, \end{align} where $n,k = -j, -j+1, \ldots, j-1, j$, $j =2N+1$, $\hat{x} \ket{x_n} = an\ket{x_n}$, $\hat{p} \ket{p_k} = 2\pi \hbar k/(aN) \ket{p_k}$, and $N$ is the Hilbert space's dimension (see Ref. \cite{DelaTorre2003a} for a detailed description of the notation).
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
nodes.origin_citation: de la Torre & Goyeneche 2003 [DelaTorre2003a]; standard in finite-dimensional QM literature
nodes.statement_short: $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$ are defined by eigenbases with $\langle x_n|p_k\rangle = e^{i2\pi nk/N}/\sqrt{N}$, eigenvalues $an$ and $2\pi\hbar k/(aN)$.

nodes.name: Defining relation of coordinate and momentum eigenvectors
nodes.statement: \langle x_n \ket{p_k} = \exp(i2\pi n k /N) / \sqrt{N},
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
nodes.label: Deff_PX_as_MUBS

nodes.name: Mutually unbiased bases
nodes.statement: According to Eq. (\ref{Deff_PX_as_MUBS}), the coordinate and momentum eigenvectors form mutually unbiased bases, which means that if a system is prepared in a state from one of the bases, then all outcomes of the measurement with respect to the other basis are equally probable.
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
differentia: if a system is prepared in a state from one of the bases, then all outcomes of the measurement with respect to the other basis are equally probable

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional Schr\"{o}dinger equation
nodes.statement: i\hbar \ket{d\Psi(t)/dt} = \hat{H} \ket{\Psi(t)},
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
nodes.label: Sch_Eq_General_Form

nodes.name: Hamiltonian $\hat{H} = \hat{p}^2/(2m) + U(\hat{x})$
nodes.statement: \hat{H} = \hat{p}^2/(2m) + U(\hat{x})
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
nodes.label: Infinite_Dim_Form_Hamiltonian

nodes.name: Tacit finite-dimensional Hamiltonian (infinite-dimensional form with MUB operators)
nodes.statement: First, the Hamiltonian \begin{align} \hat{H} = \hat{p}^2/(2m) + U(\hat{x}) \end{align} can be adapted with the specification that $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$ are defined by Eq. (\ref{Deff_PX_as_MUBS}). This is nearly a tacit definition of the Hamiltonian in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics.
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
nodes.origin_citation: tacit in the finite-dimensional QM literature
nodes.statement_short: Take $\hat{H} = \hat{p}^2/(2m) + U(\hat{x})$ with $\hat x,\hat p$ the mutually-unbiased-basis operators.
nodes.definiendum: the Hamiltonian in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics

nodes.name: Finite-difference Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: An alternative definition of $\hat{H}$, widely employed in numerical calculations (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Kimball1934}), is obtained once the term $\hat{p}^2/(2m)$, proportional to the second derivative in the infinite-dimensional coordinate representation, is approximated by finite differences.
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\hat{p}^2/(2m)$ (the second derivative) by its finite-difference approximation.

nodes.name: The two finite-dimensional Hamiltonians differ but share the $N \to \infty$ limit
nodes.statement: These two forms of the $N$-dimensional Hamiltonians are significantly different even though they converge to the same limit as $N \to \infty$.
nodes.section: Mathematical Background

nodes.name: Operational Dynamic Modeling (ODM)
nodes.statement: To answer this question, we employ Operational Dynamic Modeling (ODM) \cite{Bondar2011c}, a universal and systematic framework for deriving equations of motion from the evolution of the dynamical average values.
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
differentia: for deriving equations of motion from the evolution of the dynamical average values

nodes.name: Ehrenfest theorems
nodes.statement: m\frac{d}{dt} \bra{\Psi(t)} \hat{x} \ket{\Psi(t)} & = \bra{\Psi(t)} \hat{p} \ket{\Psi(t)}, \\ \frac{d}{dt} \bra{\Psi(t)} \hat{p} \ket{\Psi(t)} & = \bra{\Psi(t)} -U'(\hat{x}) \ket{\Psi(t)},
nodes.section: Mathematical Background
nodes.origin_citation: Ehrenfest theorems (classical result; as used in Bondar et al. 2012 [Bondar2011c])
nodes.statement_short: Ehrenfest theorems: $m\,d\langle\hat x\rangle/dt=\langle\hat p\rangle$ and $d\langle\hat p\rangle/dt=\langle -U'(\hat x)\rangle$.
nodes.label: EhrenfestTh1

nodes.name: Stone's theorem
nodes.statement: Stone's theorem (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Reed1980, Araujo2008}) guarantees the uniqueness of the Hermitian operator $\hat{H}$ in Eq. (\ref{Sch_Eq_General_Form}).
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
conclusions: guarantees the uniqueness of the Hermitian operator $\hat{H}$ in Eq. (\ref{Sch_Eq_General_Form})

nodes.name: ODM commutator equations for the Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: im \commut{\hat{H}, \hat{x}} &= \hbar \hat{p}, \\ i\commut{\hat{H}, \hat{p}} &= -\hbar U'(\hat{x}).
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: ODM applied to the Ehrenfest theorems gives $im[\hat H,\hat x]=\hbar\hat p$ and $i[\hat H,\hat p]=-\hbar U'(\hat x)$.
nodes.label: First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian

nodes.name: The ODM commutator equations have no non-trivial finite-dimensional solutions
nodes.statement: We shall demonstrate below that Eqs. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) cannot be satisfied by non-trivial finite-dimensional operators.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
conclusions: cannot be satisfied by non-trivial finite-dimensional operators

nodes.name: Theorem 1: nonexistence of the free particle in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics
nodes.statement: Assume $\hat{p}$ and $\hat{H}$ are non-zero finite-dimensional Hermitian operators. If $\commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{p} } = 0$ then there is no finite-dimensional linear operator $\hat{x}$ such that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: If non-zero Hermitian $\hat H$, $\hat p$ commute, no finite-dimensional $\hat x$ satisfies $i[\hat H,\hat x]=\hat p$.
assumptions: Assume $\hat{p}$ and $\hat{H}$ are non-zero finite-dimensional Hermitian operators.
conclusions: there is no finite-dimensional linear operator $\hat{x}$ such that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$
nodes.label: NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Let $\ket{E_n}$ denote a joint eigenvector of $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{p}$ such that $\hat{H} \ket{E_n} = E_n \ket{E_n}$ and $\hat{p} \ket{E_n} = p_n \ket{E_n}$. Assuming that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$, one obtains \begin{align} i \bra{E_n} \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } \ket{E_m} = i (E_n - E_m) \bra{E_n} \hat{x} \ket{E_m} = p_m \langle E_n \ket{E_m}, \end{align} $\forall n,m$. The special case of this identity, when $n=m$, reads $p_m = 0$, $\forall m$. This contradicts the assumption that $\hat{p}$ is a non-zero matrix.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $i[\hat H,\hat x]=\hat p$ between joint eigenvectors of $\hat H,\hat p$; the diagonal case forces $p_m=0$, contradicting $\hat p\neq 0$.

nodes.name: Joint eigenbasis and sandwiched commutator
nodes.statement: Let $\ket{E_n}$ denote a joint eigenvector of $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{p}$ such that $\hat{H} \ket{E_n} = E_n \ket{E_n}$ and $\hat{p} \ket{E_n} = p_n \ket{E_n}$. Assuming that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$, one obtains \begin{align} i \bra{E_n} \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } \ket{E_m} = i (E_n - E_m) \bra{E_n} \hat{x} \ket{E_m} = p_m \langle E_n \ket{E_m}, \end{align} $\forall n,m$.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Take joint eigenvectors of $\hat H$ and $\hat p$, assume $i[\hat H,\hat x]=\hat p$, and take matrix elements.

nodes.name: Diagonal case gives $p_m = 0$
nodes.statement: The special case of this identity, when $n=m$, reads $p_m = 0$, $\forall m$.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Set $n=m$: every momentum eigenvalue vanishes.

nodes.name: Contradiction with $\hat p \neq 0$
nodes.statement: This contradicts the assumption that $\hat{p}$ is a non-zero matrix.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Conclude: contradicts $\hat p\neq 0$.

nodes.name: Physical meaning of Theorem 1: no free particle, confinement by a force
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem} physically implies the nonexistence of the ``free'' particle in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics. This statement is also a consequence of probability conservation, closely linked to Stone's theorem. If the wave function's normalization is constant and $\hat{x}$ is finite-dimensional, then the particle's motion is confined to the spatial interval bound by the smallest and largest eigenvalues of $\hat{x}$. This confinement must be realized by some force. Since standalone Eq. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) is solvable with respect to $\hat{H}$ [see Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) below], then $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{p} }/\hbar$ from Eq. (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) can be taken as the definition of this confining force. Note that the Ehrenfest theorems do not hold for a particle in a box even in the infinite-dimensional case \cite{Alonso2000}.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1 means no free particle exists in finite dimensions; the motion is confined by a force identified with $i[\hat H,\hat p]/\hbar$.

nodes.name: Confining force
nodes.statement: Since standalone Eq. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) is solvable with respect to $\hat{H}$ [see Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) below], then $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{p} }/\hbar$ from Eq. (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) can be taken as the definition of this confining force.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: The confining force is defined as $i[\hat H,\hat p]/\hbar$ from the second ODM equation.

nodes.name: Theorem 2: no finite-dimensional derivative-as-commutator
nodes.statement: There are no finite-dimensional operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ such that \begin{align} \commut{ f(\hat{A}), \hat{B} } = f'(\hat{A}) \end{align} for any ``good'' function $f(z)$.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: No finite-dimensional $\hat A,\hat B$ satisfy $[f(\hat A),\hat B]=f'(\hat A)$ for all good $f$.
conclusions: There are no finite-dimensional operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ such that \begin{align} \commut{ f(\hat{A}), \hat{B} } = f'(\hat{A}) \end{align} for any ``good'' function $f(z)$.
nodes.label: NoDiffAsCommutator_Theorem

nodes.name: Derivative-as-commutator relation $\commut{ f(\hat{A}), \hat{B} } = f'(\hat{A})$
nodes.statement: \commut{ f(\hat{A}), \hat{B} } = f'(\hat{A})
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.label: NoDiffAsCommutator_Eq1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let a function of an operator be defined as (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Nazaikinskii1992}) \begin{align} f(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \quad f'(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int ik g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \notag \end{align} where $g(k)$ is the Fourier transform of a function $f(z)$. The correctness of Eq. (\ref{NoDiffAsCommutator_Eq1}) implies \begin{align} \commut{ e^{ik\hat{A}}, \hat{B} } = ik e^{ik\hat{A}}. \end{align} Differentiating the last identity with respect to $k$ and setting $k=0$, we reach the contradiction $\commut{ \hat{A}, \hat{B} } = 1$.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Write $f(\hat A)$ as a Fourier integral of $e^{ik\hat A}$, specialise the identity to $e^{ik\hat A}$, differentiate at $k=0$ to get $[\hat A,\hat B]=1$, impossible in finite dimensions.

nodes.name: Recall the definition of a function of an operator
nodes.statement: Let a function of an operator be defined as (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Nazaikinskii1992}) \begin{align} f(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \quad f'(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int ik g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \notag \end{align} where $g(k)$ is the Fourier transform of a function $f(z)$.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Define $f(\hat A)$ and $f'(\hat A)$ via the Fourier transform $g(k)$ of $f$.

nodes.name: Specialise the identity to $e^{ik\hat{A}}$
nodes.statement: The correctness of Eq. (\ref{NoDiffAsCommutator_Eq1}) implies \begin{align} \commut{ e^{ik\hat{A}}, \hat{B} } = ik e^{ik\hat{A}}. \end{align}
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: The assumed identity gives $[e^{ik\hat A},\hat B]=ik\,e^{ik\hat A}$.

nodes.name: Differentiate at $k=0$ to reach $[\hat A,\hat B]=1$
nodes.statement: Differentiating the last identity with respect to $k$ and setting $k=0$, we reach the contradiction $\commut{ \hat{A}, \hat{B} } = 1$.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate in $k$ at $k=0$: $[\hat A,\hat B]=1$, impossible for finite matrices.

nodes.name: Function of an operator
nodes.statement: Let a function of an operator be defined as (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Nazaikinskii1992}) \begin{align} f(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \quad f'(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int ik g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \notag \end{align} where $g(k)$ is the Fourier transform of a function $f(z)$.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: $f(\hat A) := \int g(k) e^{ik\hat A}dk$ with $g$ the Fourier transform of $f$; $f'(\hat A)$ likewise with $ik\,g(k)$.

nodes.name: Consequences of Theorem 2: nonsolvability and two definitions of potential force
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{NoDiffAsCommutator_Theorem} establishes not only the nonsolvability of Eq. (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) but also two nonequivalent definitions ($\hat{F} = - U'(\hat{x})$ and $\hat{F} = i\commut{U(\hat{x}), \hat{p}}/\hbar$) of a potential force $\hat{F}$ in a finite-dimensional framework. The latter definition should be preferred due to the comment after Theorem \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem}.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2 shows the second ODM equation is unsolvable and that $-U'(\hat x)$ and $i[U(\hat x),\hat p]/\hbar$ are inequivalent forces; prefer the latter.

nodes.name: Potential force $\hat{F}$ in a finite-dimensional framework
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{NoDiffAsCommutator_Theorem} establishes not only the nonsolvability of Eq. (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) but also two nonequivalent definitions ($\hat{F} = - U'(\hat{x})$ and $\hat{F} = i\commut{U(\hat{x}), \hat{p}}/\hbar$) of a potential force $\hat{F}$ in a finite-dimensional framework.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Liouvillian $\hat{L}$ (classical dynamics' generator)
nodes.statement: As thoroughly elaborated in Ref. \cite{Bondar2011c}, the Liouvillian $\hat{L}$, the classical dynamics' generator, is a solution of the equations: $im\commut{ \hat{L}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$ and $i\commut{\hat{L}, \hat{p}} = -U'(\hat{x})$ with commuting $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
differentia: is a solution of the equations: $im\commut{ \hat{L}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$ and $i\commut{\hat{L}, \hat{p}} = -U'(\hat{x})$ with commuting $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$

nodes.name: Theorem 3: nonexistence of the finite-dimensional Liouvillian
nodes.statement: Let $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$ be non-zero finite-dimensional Hermitian operators with $\commut{\hat{x}, \hat{p}} = 0$. There is no finite-dimensional operator $\hat{L}$ such that $i\commut{ \hat{L}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Commuting non-zero Hermitian $\hat x,\hat p$ admit no finite-dimensional $\hat L$ with $i[\hat L,\hat x]=\hat p$ (no finite-dimensional classical mechanics).
assumptions: Let $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$ be non-zero finite-dimensional Hermitian operators with $\commut{\hat{x}, \hat{p}} = 0$.
conclusions: There is no finite-dimensional operator $\hat{L}$ such that $i\commut{ \hat{L}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$.
nodes.label: NoFiniteDimClassicalMecahnics

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Up to the notation ($\hat{H} \leftrightarrow \hat{x}$ and $\hat{x} \leftrightarrow \hat{L}$), this theorem is the same as Theorem \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem}.
nodes.section: Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Identical to Theorem 1 after renaming $\hat H\leftrightarrow\hat x$ and $\hat x\leftrightarrow\hat L$.

nodes.name: Numerical accuracy is independent of the Ehrenfest theorem
nodes.statement: We shall now show that the accuracy of numerical calculations appears not to depend on whether a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian obeys the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}). Even though we analyze a specific system with a few different choices for its Hamiltonian, the conclusions are universal because the root of the problem lies in the nonexistence of bounded operators obeying the canonical commutation relation.
nodes.section: Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
nodes.statement_short: Numerical accuracy does not depend on whether the finite-dimensional Hamiltonian obeys the first Ehrenfest theorem.
conclusions: the accuracy of numerical calculations appears not to depend on whether a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian obeys the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1})

nodes.name: Most general Hamiltonian obeying the first Ehrenfest theorem
nodes.statement: \bra{x_k} \hat{H}^{\star} \ket{x_l} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} U(x_k) + C & \mbox{if } k=l \\ \frac{i \hbar \bra{x_k} \hat{p} \ket{x_l} }{m(x_k - x_l)} &\mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right.
nodes.section: Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
nodes.statement_short: For Hermitian non-degenerate $\hat x$, the solutions of $im[\hat H,\hat x]=\hbar\hat p$ are $\hat H^\star$ with diagonal $U(x_k)+C$ and off-diagonal $i\hbar\langle x_k|\hat p|x_l\rangle/(m(x_k-x_l))$.
assumptions: Assuming $\hat{x}$ is Hermitian and has a non-degenerate spectrum
where $\hat{x} \ket{x_l} = x_l \ket{x_l}$ and $C$ is an arbitrary real constant
conclusions: For any definition of the momentum operator $\hat{p}$, Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) provides the most general Hamiltonian obeying the first Ehrenfest theorem [Eq. (\ref{EhrenfestTh1})].
nodes.label: Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian

nodes.name: Finite-difference momentum operator $\hat{p}_{fd}$
nodes.statement: Choosing $\hat{x}$ with equally spaced eigenvalues (with the step $a$) and utilizing the approximation $d \Psi(x_k) /dx \approx [ \Psi(x_{k+1}) - \Psi(x_{k-1}) ] / (2a)$, we can define the momentum operator: $\bra{x_k} \hat{p}_{fd} \ket{x_l} = -i\hbar\left( \delta_{l,k+1} - \delta_{l,k-1} \right)/(2a)$.
nodes.section: Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
nodes.statement_short: Central-difference momentum: $\langle x_k|\hat p_{fd}|x_l\rangle = -i\hbar(\delta_{l,k+1}-\delta_{l,k-1})/(2a)$ on an equally spaced grid.

nodes.name: Ehrenfest-compatible finite-difference Hamiltonian $\hat{H}^{\star}_{fd}$
nodes.statement: Then, the corresponding Hamiltonian from Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}), \begin{align} \bra{x_k} \hat{H}^{\star}_{fd} \ket{x_l} = \frac{-\hbar^2}{2ma^2} \left( \delta_{l,k+1} + \delta_{l,k-1} \right) + [U(x_k) + C]\delta_{l,k}, \end{align} satisfying the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}), takes the form of the simplest finite-difference approximation for the differential operator: $-\hbar^2/(2m) d^2/dx^2 + U(x)$.
nodes.section: Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
nodes.statement_short: $\hat H^\star_{fd}$, the general Hamiltonian with $\hat p_{fd}$, is the simplest finite-difference discretisation of $-\hbar^2/(2m)d^2/dx^2+U(x)$.

nodes.name: Finite-difference Ehrenfest-compatible Hamiltonian $\hat{H}^{\star}_{fd}$
nodes.statement: \bra{x_k} \hat{H}^{\star}_{fd} \ket{x_l} = \frac{-\hbar^2}{2ma^2} \left( \delta_{l,k+1} + \delta_{l,k-1} \right) + [U(x_k) + C]\delta_{l,k},
nodes.section: Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
nodes.label: FiniteDiff_approx_Hamiltonian

nodes.name: Hamiltonians $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ and $\hat{H}_{mub}$
nodes.statement: Let $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ denote the Hamiltonian (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) after substituting $\hat{p}$ from Eq. (\ref{Deff_PX_as_MUBS}), and $\hat{H}_{mub}$ be the Hamiltonian (\ref{Infinite_Dim_Form_Hamiltonian}) with the same $\hat{p}$.
nodes.section: Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
nodes.statement_short: $\hat H^\star_{mub}$: general Ehrenfest-compatible Hamiltonian with the MUB momentum; $\hat H_{mub}$: $\hat p^2/(2m)+U(\hat x)$ with the same $\hat p$.

nodes.name: $\hat{H}_{mub}$ violates the first Ehrenfest theorem
nodes.statement: Contrary to $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$, the matrix $\hat{H}_{mub}$ does not satisfy the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}).
nodes.section: Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
conclusions: the matrix $\hat{H}_{mub}$ does not satisfy the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1})

nodes.name: Numerical comparison of $\hat{H}^{\star}_{fd}$, $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$, $\hat{H}_{mub}$ for the singular harmonic oscillator
nodes.statement: Figures \ref{Fig_SpectraComparison} and \ref{Fig_EigenvectorComparison} depict the eigenvalues and the twentieth eigenvector of the Hamiltonians $\hat{H}^{\star}_{fd}$, $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$, and $\hat{H}_{mub}$ for the oscillator, \begin{align} U(x) = \frac{\omega^2}{8} x^2 + \frac{g}{4x^2}, \qquad 0 \leqslant x < \infty, \end{align} which is exactly solvable in the infinite-dimensional case \cite{Calogero1969}. The values of the coordinate step, $a$, for $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ and $\hat{H}_{mub}$ are selected to minimize the largest eigenvalues of each Hamiltonian, which leads to the spectra of $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ and $\hat{H}_{mub}$ (for a finite $N$) best fitting the exact energy in the infinite-dimensional case [see Figs. \ref{Fig_SpectraComparison}(b) and \ref{Fig_SpectraComparison}(c)]. However, the same recipe applied to $\hat{H}_{fd}^{\star}$ does not provide a good fit, and the step size for $\hat{H}_{fd}^{\star}$ is manually adjusted to match the exact energies. This exercise demonstrates [Fig. \ref{Fig_EigenvectorComparison}(a)] that even though the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{fd}^{\star}$ reproduces the exact energy better than either $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ or $\hat{H}_{mub}$, it yields poor quality excited states. Finally, note that the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$, satisfying Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}), provides results of the same quality as $\hat{H}_{mub}$, violating Eq. (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}). These observations indicate that there is no correlation between the numerical calculations' accuracy and the Ehrenfest theorem's validity. Note, however, that any disagreement between the exact and numerical results in Figs. \ref{Fig_SpectraComparison} and \ref{Fig_EigenvectorComparison} will exponentially increase with the number of spatial dimensions.
nodes.section: Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
nodes.statement_short: 30-dimensional spectra and eigenvectors for the singular oscillator show no correlation between accuracy and validity of the Ehrenfest theorem.

nodes.name: Non-Hermitian generalization of the ODM commutator equations
nodes.statement: First, re-applying ODM to Eqs. (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}) and (\ref{EhrenfestTh2}) with the condition $\hat{H} \neq \hat{H}^{\dagger}$, the following generalizations of Eqs. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) are obtained: \begin{align} im ( \hat{H}^{\dagger} \hat{x} - \hat{x} \hat{H} ) = \hbar \hat{p}, \quad i ( \hat{H}^{\dagger} \hat{p} - \hat{p} \hat{H} ) = -\hbar U'(\hat{x}). \end{align}
nodes.section: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies
nodes.statement_short: For $\hat H\neq\hat H^\dagger$, ODM gives $im(\hat H^\dagger\hat x-\hat x\hat H)=\hbar\hat p$ and $i(\hat H^\dagger\hat p-\hat p\hat H)=-\hbar U'(\hat x)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 1: disjoint spectra of $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{H}^{\dagger}$ force $\hat{p} = \hat{x} = 0$
nodes.statement: Assume that $\hat{x}$, $\hat{p}$, and $\hat{H}$ are bounded. If $\sigma(\hat{H}^{\dagger}) \cap \sigma(\hat{H}) = \emptyset$ and \begin{align} & im ( \hat{H}^{\dagger} \hat{x} - \hat{x} \hat{H} ) = \hbar \hat{p}, \\ & \hat{H}^{\dagger} \hat{p} = \hat{p} \hat{H}, \end{align} then $\hat{p} = \hat{x} = 0$. Here, $\sigma(\hat{A})$ denotes the spectrum of an operator $\hat{A}$.
nodes.section: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies
nodes.statement_short: Bounded $\hat x,\hat p,\hat H$ with $\sigma(\hat H^\dagger)\cap\sigma(\hat H)=\emptyset$ solving the non-Hermitian free equations must vanish.
nodes.label: NonHermitian_Lemma1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: First, we employ the Rosenblum theorem \cite{Rosenblum1956} (see Theorem 9.3 in Ref. \cite{Bhatia1997}) to Eq. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and then employ Eq. (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) to show \begin{align} im\hat{x} =& \frac{\hbar}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} d\xi ( \hat{H}^{\dagger} - \xi )^{-1} \hat{p} ( \hat{H} - \xi )^{-1} \notag\\ =& \frac{\hbar}{2\pi i} \hat{p} \oint_{\Gamma} d\xi ( \hat{H} - \xi )^{-2} = 0, \end{align} where $\Gamma$ denotes a union of closed contours in the complex plane with total winding numbers $1$ around $\sigma(\hat{H}^{\dagger})$ and $0$ around $\sigma(\hat{H})$.
nodes.section: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies
nodes.statement_short: Solve the Sylvester equation for $\hat x$ by the Rosenblum theorem as a contour integral, then use $\hat H^\dagger\hat p=\hat p\hat H$ to collapse it to zero.

nodes.name: Theorem 4: no free particle for non-Hermitian finite-dimensional Hamiltonians
nodes.statement: Assume i) $\hat{H}$, $\hat{x}$, and $\hat{p}$ are finite-dimensional operators satisfying Eqs. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}); ii) $\lim_{t \to +\infty} \left| \langle \Psi(t) \ket{\Psi(t)} \right| < \infty$, where $\ket{\Psi(t)}$ is a solution of Eq. (\ref{Sch_Eq_General_Form}); iii) the eigenvectors $\{ \ket{E_n} \}_{n=1}^N$ ($\hat{H}\ket{E_n} = E_n \ket{E_n}$, $n \in I \coloneqq \{1,2,\ldots,N\}$) span the entire Hilbert space. Then, $\hat{p} = 0$.
nodes.section: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies
nodes.statement_short: A finite-dimensional non-Hermitian $\hat H$ with bounded norm evolution and complete eigenvectors solving the free-particle equations forces $\hat p=0$.
assumptions: i) $\hat{H}$, $\hat{x}$, and $\hat{p}$ are finite-dimensional operators satisfying Eqs. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian})
ii) $\lim_{t \to +\infty} \left| \langle \Psi(t) \ket{\Psi(t)} \right| < \infty$, where $\ket{\Psi(t)}$ is a solution of Eq. (\ref{Sch_Eq_General_Form})
iii) the eigenvectors $\{ \ket{E_n} \}_{n=1}^N$ ($\hat{H}\ket{E_n} = E_n \ket{E_n}$, $n \in I \coloneqq \{1,2,\ldots,N\}$) span the entire Hilbert space
nodes.label: NonHermitian_Theorem1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Suppose $\hat{p} \neq 0$. According to Lyapunov stability theory \cite{Lyapunov1992}, the second assumption implies that $\Im(E_n) \leqslant 0$, $\forall n\in I$. Lemma \ref{NonHermitian_Lemma1} guarantees that $\hat{H}$ has at least a single real eigenvalue. Introduce $R \coloneqq \{ n \in I \, | \, \Im(E_n) = 0 \} \neq \emptyset$ -- the set of the real eigenvalues' indices. ``Sandwiching'' Eqs. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) leads to \begin{align} & im ( E_k^* - E_l ) \bra{E_k} \hat{x} \ket{E_l} = \hbar \bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l}, \\ & ( E_k^* - E_l ) \bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l} = 0, \qquad \forall k,l \in I. \end{align} According to Eq. (\ref{NonHermTh1_Eq2}), $\bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l}$ may be non-zero only for $(k,l) \in Q \coloneqq \{ (k,l) \in R \times R \, | \, E_k = E_l \}$. However, Eq. (\ref{NonHermTh1_Eq1}) enforces $\bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l} = 0$, $\forall (k,l) \in Q$. Therefore, we reach the contradiction $\hat{p} = 0$.

nodes.statement_short: Assume $\hat p\neq0$; Lyapunov stability gives $\Im E_n\le0$, Lemma 1 gives a real eigenvalue, and sandwiching the equations between eigenvectors forces all matrix elements of $\hat p$ to vanish.

nodes.name: Nonstandard analysis as a way around the no-go theorems
nodes.statement: In particular, a key element in proving theorems \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem} and \ref{NoFiniteDimClassicalMecahnics} is the non-existence of a finite real number $r$ such that $0\cdot r \neq 0$. However, this equation has a solution if infinitesimal and infinitely-large numbers are included into the set of real numbers. Thus, some of the no-go theorems may be avoided by utilizing nonstandard analysis \cite{robert2003nonstandard, Almeida2004}, where such extensions are rigorously implemented.
nodes.section: Outlook
nodes.statement_short: The no-go proofs hinge on no finite real $r$ having $0\cdot r\neq 0$; nonstandard analysis with infinitesimals could circumvent them.
